citations.excerpt: If False, serialization of out-of-range float values (nan, inf, -inf) will result in a ValueError, in strict compliance with the JSON specification.

claims.text: When allow_nan=False, serialization of out-of-range float values (nan, inf, -inf) will result in a ValueError, in strict compliance with the JSON specification.

citations.excerpt: If True (the default), their JavaScript equivalents (NaN, Infinity, -Infinity) are used.
If allow_nan is true (the default), then NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity will be encoded as such.

claims.text: By default (allow_nan=True), NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity are encoded as their JavaScript equivalents (NaN, Infinity, -Infinity).

citations.excerpt: This behavior is not JSON specification compliant, but is consistent with most JavaScript based encoders and decoders.

claims.text: This default behavior (encoding NaN/Infinity) is not JSON specification compliant, but is consistent with most JavaScript based encoders and decoders.

citations.excerpt: # Neither of these calls raises an exception, but the results are not valid JSON >>> json.dumps(float('-inf')) '-Infinity' >>> json.dumps(float('nan')) 'NaN'

claims.text: By default, json.dumps(float('-inf')) produces '-Infinity' and json.dumps(float('nan')) produces 'NaN', without raising an exception, though the results are not valid JSON.

citations.excerpt: The RFC does not permit the representation of infinite or NaN number values. Despite that, by default, this module accepts and outputs Infinity, -Infinity, and NaN as if they were valid JSON number literal values:

claims.text: The RFC does not permit the representation of infinite or NaN number values, but by default this module accepts and outputs Infinity, -Infinity, and NaN as if they were valid JSON number literal values.

citations.excerpt: In the serializer, the allow_nan parameter can be used to alter this behavior.

claims.text: In the serializer, the allow_nan parameter can be used to alter the default behavior regarding NaN and Infinity values.
